(3d) 326 (Q.B.), the successful plaintiff sought as costs the fees paid to agent solicitors for their efforts to locate an out-of-jurisdiction medical expert. The costs were claimed as a disbursement. Johnstone J. disallowed the claim. At p. 337, her Ladyship said: This agency fee is denied for two reasons. Firstly, if allowed, this would have the demonstrated effect of increasing the total legal fees taxable against the other party above the amount prescribed by the legislature for those fees. Secondly, the professional service for locating and retaining experts is a normal task of counsel to seek such experts from outside its own city or province without utilizing an agent.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.31:4 Plans, models, copies of documents See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. Photocopying charges … within the limits of a situation involving a few copies, the financial burden of the overhead involved in producing a pleading is taken into account in fixing the fee for the work product … Let me add also that, even in the case of party-and-party costs, when numerous copies are needed it is reasonable to allow photocopying costs. Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 at 54–55 (Q.B.). In Clancy v. Gough, 2011 ABQB 778, 2011 CarswellAlta 2179, 523 A.R. 163, 59 Alta. L.R. (5th) 108, Bensler, J. commented on costs claims for printing and photocopying. At paragraphs 54–59, her Ladyship said: 54 Laser printing and photocopying are interesting categories. Clearly having the ability to print and photocopy is a necessary capability to operate any law office, so the associated costs tend to fall within the characterization of overhead. Moreover, given that many firms do actually produce most documents in-house (often using commercial quality printers and photocopiers) the cost associated with printing and photocopying is not a true disbursement paid to a third party. 55 On the other hand, the practice of law is still incredibly document intensive and paper-based, so in my view it is reasonable to allow some level of recovery for printing and photocopying directly related to a particular file. However, I do so cautiously. It seems the rate that many law offices charge for these services is out of touch with the true internal cost, or the equivalent expense that would otherwise be incurred if these services were delivered by a third party commercial printer. 56 That premise seems to apply in this case where counsel for the Defendants informed the Court that its practice is to bill each black and white printed or copied page at 30 cent(s) each, though no independent evidence was introduced in support. I take judicial notice that the commercial cost to the public for similar services is considerably less. For example, at the various Staples Copy and Print Centres around Calgary the cost of printing and photocopying ranges from 3–10 cent(s) per standard page, depending on the quantity of printing ordered. It is also worthy to note that those rates still result in profit to the commercial printer. 57 I find it unreasonable that the Defendants seek to recover from the Plaintiffs a “disbursement” at least three times higher than if the work had actually been performed by a third party. In the words of Wittmann J.A. (as he then was) “one would expect evidence that money was paid to a third party in order to qualify as a disbursement.” While I am willing to allow some level of printing and photocopying, lacking evidence as to the true cost of these services to the law firm, I am not willing to entertain a submission for an expense so out of alignment with commercial reality. If law firms are actually incurring 30 cent(s) to produce every printed or photocopied page then lawyers should be prepared to submit evidence related thereto when attempting to recover these costs from their clients, or the other party. 58 Using the rate provided by counsel and the aggregate charges for these line items on the Bill of Costs, the number of underlying pages can be mathematically calculated. In this manner I have determined the volume of laser printed and photocopied pages was 7369 and 7002, respectively. However, the cost reproducing drafts, or the cost of copying documents such as pleadings, motions and affidavits compensated under another item in the costs schedule, is not recoverable: Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 322 A.R. 307 at paras. 72–74. In oral argument counsel for the Defendants estimated that approximately 10% of the total pages produced was used to create ‘final’ documents. As such, I allow 10% of 7369 for laser printing and 10% of 7002 pages for photocopying. 59 Referring back to the publicly available Staples price list, this quantity of standard printing would cost 6 cent(s) per page. While I don't impose the same efficiencies on a law firm as might be incumbent on a commercial printer, I find 10 cent(s) per page to be reasonable in the circumstances. Reducing the rate for printing and photocopying also finds judicial support both in this Court as well as the Alberta Court of Appeal: Lynch at para. 48, Dechant v. Law Society of Alberta, 2001 ABCA 81, 277 A.R. 333 at para. 30, and Marathon Canada Ltd. at para. 53. 2. Rate for Photocopies Each case is decided individually but it is clear that one should produce evidence of the rate being suggested (either as claimant or payor). In Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 (Q.B.), at p. 56 McDonald J. said: In the present case, without the benefit of any evidence as to the actual cost of photocopying, I am prepared to recognize a cost of 15 cents a page. Still, there is no hard and fast rule, so evidence is preferable. This is so whether one seeks the disbursement or wishes to pay a lower rate. The Court of Appeal has made reference to the problems associated with a failure to provide evidence of the true cost of the disbursement sought. In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); [reconsideration refused [(1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999), 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], the court said, at p. 271: Finally, the appellants argued that the photocopy charge of 25 cents per page is not a true disbursement. They argued that the true cost of photocopying should be in the neigbourhood of 3 to 5 cents, and that any amount above this should be included in overhead costs. Unfortunately, there was no evidentiary basis for the argument and accordingly we leave it to another day whether a 25 cent charge for such disbursements is excessive. The trial judge allowed this amount as a disbursement and we do not disturb this portion of the award. In Dechant v. Stevens, 2001 ABCA 81, 2001 CarswellAlta 356, 277 A.R. 333, 89 Alta. L.R. (3d) 289; leave to appeal refused 2001 CarswellAlta 1211, [2001] 3 S.C.R. vi, a rate of $.25 per page was sought for photocopying. The court, per curiam, said: … copying is a legitimate disbursement. If [Dechant] can prove that she has paid 25 cents a page to some arm's length person, the fee should be allowed. Otherwise we order 15 cents a page. Photocopying is a difficult disbursement to address. Evidence in a given case may show that there should be no charge for photocopies for the represented litigant because the cost associated with copying is just part of the overhead of the firm which is compensated by a general costs order. Alternatively, there may be evidence in a given case as to the actual costs incurred as a result of farming out the expense to a third party. It may even be that a general costs award should be higher for the unrepresented litigant who does not receive a costs award over and above disbursements. In Fill v. Somani, 2013 ABQB 572, 2013 CarswellAlta 1858, 571 A.R. 230, Justice Shelley awarded $0.28 per photocopy page, stressing that the evidence before the Court supported the claim. Justice Shelley said, at paragraphs 61 and 63: 61 The Plaintiffs submit that the in-house photocopying costs should be awarded at the rate of $0.28 per page. This position is supported by Affidavit evidence of Jennifer Paolucci, a Legal Assistant employed by Plaintiffs' counsel. Ms. Paolucci's Affidavit details the various costs associated with the photocopying of documents and concludes that the actual costs of photocopying are approximately $0.38 per page. … 63 The Defendants do not provide any evidence which suggests that the analysis undertaken by Ms. Paolucci was erroneous in any way. Where a party does not provide evidence to support a higher amount, Courts have arbitrarily set an amount. However, where there is evidence to support a higher number, Courts have awarded it. Here, Ms. Paolucci's evidence confirms actual photocopying costs of $0.38 per page. I conclude that the requested amount of $0.28 per page has been proven, since there is no evidence or analysis to contradict it. Accordingly, the amount claimed will be awarded. 3. Meaning of “copies of documents” In Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R. 307, 9 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, the successful plaintiff sought $14,626.92 in photocopying charges. Fraser J. allowed $2500.00, and discussed the meaning of the phrase “copies of documents” at pp. 326–328: [72] The cost of producing copies of documents required for use in the trial including expert reports, exhibits, and arguments and other documents which must be served, is in my view a cost which can be passed on. However, the cost of repeated photocopying of drafts of documents prepared for use in the action such as arguments, or of other miscellaneous documents such as letters, is not. [73] Rule 600(1)(a)(iv) governs the right to claim the cost of photocopying as a disbursement. … [74] The reference to “copies of documents” in my opinion is to final copies of existing documents such as those listed in paragraph 72 above. It does not cover copies of drafts. Nor does it cover “the preparation of copies of pleadings, notices of motion, affidavits, orders and so on which is covered by Rule 605(3) and cannot be included if the copy in question is a copy of a document used in completing some step already covered by another item included in the Bill of Costs”. Per McDonald, J. (as he then was), in Ukrainian (Edmonton) Credit Union Ltd. v. 258753 Alberta Ltd., Gourdine and Olsen (1984), 60 A.R. 148 (Q.B.).

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.31:5 Other Charges See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. Lost Wages In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 296 (Q.B.); [varied on other grounds (1997) 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); reconsideration refused (1998) 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999) 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], McMahon J. allowed a claim for conduct money to include amounts paid to witnesses as compensation of wages lost due to attendance at trial. Special circumstances would appear to be necessary to warrant such an award. At p. 303, his Lordship said: The defence paid conduct money for their witnesses and, as well, paid travel accommodation and meal expenses where incurred. In a few cases they appear to have paid a day's wages lost for attendance at trial. Given the number of witnesses and the obvious scheduling difficulties in a lengthy trial of this kind, these disbursements do not seem inordinate. I specifically allow the payment for lost wages where paid instead of the daily witness fee provided by Sched. C. I do so because of my findings as detailed in the Reasons for Judgment that the tenants and former tenants (who comprised most of the witnesses) had been poorly treated by the plaintiffs. They have suffered enough loss without having to incur further loss as a consequence of giving testimony. 2. Conduct Money For One's Own Officers and Employees In Parrish & Heimbecker Ltd. v. All Peace Auctions Ltd. (2002), 326 A.R. 383, a defendant was successful at trial. The defendant sought as part of its costs conduct money for its employees and officers who attended examinations for discovery and trial. An informal agreement had been reached by counsel to produce officers and employees at discoveries without the need of formal appointments and without payment of conduct money. At p. 389, Phillips J. said: W.A. Stevenson and J.E. Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, vol. 2 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1996) states, at 1938, that parties are entitled to conduct money as part of a costs award regardless of whether a demand for conduct money was made. Further, an agreement between counsel to forego formal appointments and the payment of conduct money at the time, does not prevent a party from seeking costs in this regard. Accordingly, I find that All Peace is entitled to conduct money for the attendance of its employees and officers at trial and examinations for discovery for those days when evidence was being given by these individuals. 3. Lump Sum Costs In Wener v. Wener, an unreported decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal rendered June 8, 1971, Calgary Appeal Number 7912, the court concluded that the discretion to award a lump sum in lieu of taxing costs can be exercised only where the trial judge has full information about the work done and the disbursements incurred. If true for taxable costs, it must also be true for solicitor/client costs. Markdale Ltd. v. Ducharme (1998), 238 A.R. 98 (Q.B.), at 106, per Bielby J. [leave to appeal refused (1998), 238 A.R. 321 (Q.B.)].

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.31 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: The primary purpose of a costs award is to partly indemnify the successful party for the costs of the litigation: British Columbia (Minister of Forests) v. Okanagan Indian Band, 2003 SCC 71 at paras. 21, 26, [2003] 3 SCR 371. Since a self-represented litigant does not incur any legal fees, the ordinary objective of indemnification is not achieved. Costs awards do, however, achieve other purposes: they can be used to encourage settlement, or to prevent frivolous, vexatious or harassing litigation, and they can also be used to encourage economy and efficiency during litigation. Rule 10.31(5) ensures that those purposes of a costs award can be achieved even where a party is self-represented. 9 Previous decisions have observed that awarding costs to self-represented litigants raises difficult policy issues. The expectation that costs might be received can actually invert the usual objectives of costs, by encouraging litigation and discouraging settlement “because of an anticipated windfall to the unrepresented litigant that could result from a costs award”: Dechant v. Law Society of Alberta, 2001 ABCA 81 at para. 15, 89 Alta LR (3d) 289, 277 AR 333. As Dechant observed at paras. 16–7, self-represented litigants do not necessarily bear a greater personal burden: 16 It is true that unrepresented litigants expend time and effort presenting their law suits. Represented litigants, however, also sacrifice a considerable amount of their own time and effort for which no compensation is paid. Any award of costs is merely a partial reimbursement for their lawyer's fees. As noted, an award of costs to represented litigants should never be higher than their solicitor-client fees, which are only awarded in exceptional circumstances. Thus, applying an identical costs schedule to both represented and unrepresented litigants will work an inequity against the represented litigant who, even with an award of costs, will be left with some legal fees to pay and no compensation for a personal investment of time. What the Rules do provide is that both kinds of litigants are to be paid for their out-of-pocket expenses. 17 … Applying an identical costs schedule to the unrepresented litigants, who have no out-of-pocket expenses for the legal fee portion of the suit, effectively awards fees for their own time and work. In short, self-litigation could become an occupation. For these reasons, a self-represented litigant should generally not receive costs unless that would serve one of the policy reasons for which costs awards are made. 10 The appellant Simonson suggests he should receive two-thirds of the assessable costs during the time he was self-represented. Such an award, however, would still represent an indemnity for expenses that were never incurred. While it is undoubtedly true that Simonson took time away from his business affairs to attend the trial, that is true of most litigants, whether they are self-represented or not. There is no evidence on this record that Simonson exercised any special skill during the trial (such as briefing the law, or arguing complex issues), nor that he was burdened more than the average litigant. In the circumstances, it is appropriate that for the portion of the trial when he was self-represented he only receive assessable disbursements. In Melanson v. Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board Appeals Commission), 2011 ABQB 367, 511 A.R. 178, 2011 CarswellAlta 2516, 64 Alta. L.R. (5th) 192, Justice Lee concluded that in the action before him the Workers' Compensation Board was a party under R. 10.28. He then commented (at paragraph 25) on R. 10.31(5): 25 I agree with the depiction of a self-represented litigant offered by the WCB as accurate. I am of the view that Rule 10.31(5) of the Rules of Court contemplates individual persons who are parties to an action and represent themselves without the services of legal counsel. In this action, both the WCB and the Appeals Commission as creatures of statute, were represented by legal counsel: see, WCA, ss. 2(1), 3 and 10. It will constitute an unjustifiable stretch of the term if a creature of statute provided with services of legal counsel on judicial appeal before the court is construed as a self represented litigant. The following cases were decided before R. 10.31(5) came into being, and show that even then unrepresented litigants were sometimes awarded costs. It is clear that the Court of Queen's Bench in Alberta recognizes the granting of costs to unrepresented litigants. I agree with and I adopt the reasoning of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Skidmore v. Blackmore[(1995), 122 D.L.R. (4th) 330]… The awarding of costs in this province, as in British Columbia, is discretionary … Furthermore, it is clear from the Rules of Court that the reasons for awarding costs are beyond mere indemnification. Rule 601(1) and Rule 174 show that costs also exist to encourage settlement and discourage misconduct on the part of litigants. Thus, I find that the Applicant is entitled to costs in this case despite the fact that she was unrepresented by counsel some of the time. C. (A.R.) v. C. (L.L.) (1999), 72 Alta. L.R. (3d) 300 (Q.B.), at 306–307, per Marceau J. In Edmonton (Police Service) v. Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2019 ABQB 864, 2019 CarswellAlta 2434, Justice Graesser said: [30] In summary, I note that in Alberta, nothing has really changed since my decision in LL v GB, 2009 ABQB 322, which was decided before the 2010 Rules of Court changes. The approach has not changed with the new Rules of Court, and the Alberta courts have not followed along the Ontario or British Columbia lines. I said in LL at paragraph 67: [67] I think the following principles are applicable to the award of costs in favour of a successful self-represented litigant: 1. There is no automatic rule entitling a self-represented litigant to costs. While there is a presumption in favour of awarding costs on a party and party basis to a successful represented litigant, a self-represented litigant bears a stronger onus of establishing an entitlement to costs; 2. In determining entitlement, the Court should have regard to the factors set out in Dechant; 3. To achieve fairness, a self-represented party's time is a minor factor in the consideration of costs, and then only to the extent that the self-represented party has spent more time on the matter than one would expect a represented party to have spent. 4. The Court's discretion should be exercised after an analysis of the Dechant factors; 5. Only after the Court has exercised its discretion in favour of awarding costs to a self-represented litigant should the Court determine the quantum of costs; 6. Schedule C is a guide to determining quantum, but the Court may exercise a discretion to award a lump sum, or all or a portion of Schedule C costs; and 7. The Court should try to avoid turning the assessment of costs into a further trial. [31] I will offer a few further observations: 1. It would be very rare for costs in favour of a self-represented litigant to exceed the amount of costs that would be awarded to a represented party in the same case; in other words, if Schedule C column 1 would normally be appropriate, the self-represented litigant should not receive more than that even if his or her lost opportunity costs exceeded that amount; 2. It is difficult if not impossible to reconcile the principles in Dechant and Hogarth with a self-represented litigant being awarded double costs under Rule 4.29, or enhanced costs unless the self-represented litigant can demonstrate that such amounts are still within what the litigant can prove on balance is within his or her lost opportunity; 3. Issues such having been taken unfair advantage of procedurally or misconduct by the other party during the litigation (such as those things usually advanced by parties seeking solicitor and client costs or enhanced costs) may justify in appropriate circumstances some measure of punitive cost award in favour of a self-represented litigant. 4. I think there is a clear distinction to be made between litigation initiated by a self-represented litigant or maintained by the litigant him or herself after counsel has withdrawn for whatever reason, and a litigant responding to litigation brought against him or her. It seems to me that there is less worry about a litigant turning the litigation into an occupation when the self-represented litigant is the defendant or respondent. The litigant may have little choice but to represent him or herself for financial reasons. Legal aid is rarely available for civil litigants outside the family law area, and even in that area is limited to very poor litigants. A sued person has no choice but to respond, and faces a system where his or her legal costs will be fully indemnified on success only in very exceptional circumstances. 2. Costs for Intervenors In Auer v. Auer, 2021 ABQB 860, 2021 CarswellAlta 2720, Mr. Auer unsuccessfully challenged the jurisdictional foundation of the Federal Child Support Guidelines. The Attorney General of Canada was an Intervenor in those proceedings and sought costs against Mr. Auer. Justice Rothwell discussed when costs should be awarded to an Intervenor: [13] Mr. Auer cites the decision of Stoney Tribal Council v PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd, 2000 ABCA 164 at para 2 [Stoney Tribal Council] for the proposition that intervenors are generally not entitled to costs. In that case Chevron Canada Resources (Chevron) was granted intervenor status to respond to a constitutional issue raised by the Stoney Tribal Council. The Stoney Tribal Council withdrew its constitutional challenge and Chevron did not participate in the appeal. The Court declined to grant Chevron its intervention costs. [14] The AGC cited Lynnview Ridge Residents' Action Committee v Imperial Oil Limited, 2005 ABCA 375 [Lynnview] and Canadian Union of Postal Workers v Her Majesty in Right of Canada, 2017 ONSC 6503 [CUPW] in support of the proposition that costs, in appropriate circumstances, may be awarded to intervenors. [15] Intervenors are generally granted intervenor status to offer an argument that is useful and different and/or to assist the Court. They generally take the record as they find it and their participation is limited: Suncor Energy Inc v Unifor, Local 707 A, 2014 ABQB 555. [16] In Lynnview the Alberta Court of Appeal noted the following considerations with respect to the appropriateness of awarding costs to an intervenor, at para 25: I conclude that there are circumstances where an intervener with a special interest should be awarded costs. Although the circumstances will vary, the factors to be taken into account in determining whether it is appropriate to deviate from the general rule include: • Has the intervener contributed to the court's deliberations by adding a viewpoint that otherwise would not have been considered? Alternatively, did the parties themselves present the same arguments or points of view? • Is there legislation relevant to the case to suggest whether the intervener has a special interest or an important role to play? • What is the nature of the intervener's special interest? The interest might be financial, proprietary, non-pecuniary or other. [17] The Ontario Court of Superior Justice in CUPW identified six factors for consideration in its decision, at para 31: i. What is the nature and extent of the intervener's interest in the issues that were before the court and in the outcome of the proceeding? ii. What was the nature and extent of the intervener's involvement in the proceeding? iii. What are the intervener's resources? iv. Was the intervener successful on the merits? v. Did one of the parties anticipate or provoke the intervener's involvement? vi. Did the terms of the order granting leave to intervene address the possibility of a cost award? [18] I note that there are similarities between the Lynnview and CUPW factors but I will focus primarily on the Lynnview factors as they emanate from the Court of Appeal of Alberta. In the end, costs were awarded to the Attorney General on Column 2 of Schedule C. 3. Number of Bills of Costs when Multiple Defendants In Kucher v. Seaboard Life Assurance Co. (1997), 208 A.R. 1 (Q.B.), the plaintiff provided two bills of costs: one in each of two actions tried together and commenced by it in respect of two insurance policies (one issued by Seaboard and one issued by CIBC). Clarke J., at p. 7, said: It was the plaintiff's position that they had to fight both actions, both CIBC and Seaboard had counsel and both counsel participated in the defence of the claim, so it was appropriate to award separate costs against each of those parties as represented by the separate bills of costs… I have concluded that where there are items of costs such as commencing proceedings by Statement of Claim which are clearly individual to each of the defendants a bill of costs is appropriate for each defendant. On the other hand, where actions were undertaken for the benefit of all of the defendants and it was agreed that the activity could be used by all of the defendants then those costs should be prorated amongst the defendants involved. Dealing more specifically with the trial, I am satisfied that there should be one bill of costs for the actvities at trial. The defendants presented their case as a common case and there was no significant overlap in any of the actions taken by the counsel for each of the defendants. 4. Schedule C and Appeals from Provincial Court In Yi v. Varadi (c.o.b. Key Homes Inspections), 2013 ABQB 441, 2013 CarswellAlta 1508, 560 A.R. 297, 98 Alta. L.R. (5th) 415, Justice Lee held that Schedule C applies to appeals from Provincial Court to the Court of Queen's Bench. In his reasons, his Lordship acknowledged that there is a disagreement on the topic amongst his judicial colleagues. He said, at paragraph 9: 9 I conclude that the Schedule C costs are still appropriate and applicable for an appeal of a Provincial Court Decision to the Court of Queen's Bench, notwithstanding that there is no specific provision for this in Schedule C. Although my colleague Veit, J. generally disagreed with this proposition in Condominium Plan 8022962 v. Malinowsky, 2005 ABQB 346, and Mahar v. Edmonton Dream Cleaners Ltd, 2005 ABQB 37, I conclude that the quantum of Schedule C column 1 costs are relatively modest, and the categories provided for in Schedule C for an appeal are generally equally applicable to appeals to the Court of Queen's Bench from the Provincial Court. Specifically I conclude that the Schedule C costs are appropriate for an appeal of a Provincial Court Decision to the Court of Queen's Bench in the current matter given it's (sic) complexity and issues of law. Justice Pentelechuk said, in Genge v. Centron Residential Corp., 2014 ABQB 50, 2014 CarswellAlta 270, at paragraph 27: …Yi v. Varadi, 2013 ABQB 441, at para 9, provides authority for the award of Schedule C costs for an Appeal of a Provincial Court decision to the Court of Queen's Bench, notwithstanding that there is no specific provision for this in Schedule C. . . . . . 5. Costs and the Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act In Ezzedine v. Dalgard (2007), 73 Alta. L.R. (4th) 58 (Alta. Q.B.), the Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act was included as a defendant in a motor vehicle accident action because the uninsured defendant Dalgard had been noted in default. At the end of the trial, Mackin J. ruled that the Administrator was entitled to costs. The Administrator sought costs based on the amounts claimed (Column 5) as opposed to the Administrator's statutorily set monetary exposure (Column 3). The learned trial judge held that the Administrator was only entitled to Column 3 costs. Macklin J. said, at p. 68: 35 In my view, the Administrator is only entitled to those costs that reflect its actual exposure in the case. It is conceded that the Administrator's maximum total exposure, regardless of the amounts that might be awarded to the Plaintiffs, is $200,000. While the Statements of Claim seek damages exceeding the limits of the Administrator's exposure, all parties were fully aware at all times that the Administrator would never be responsible for any payment of damages exceeding the prescribed limit. 36 The difference between the Administrator as a Defendant and other Defendants who would be entitled to have their costs determined against the Plaintiff on the basis of the amount claimed is that other Defendants' exposure is not limited as is that of the Administrator. Further, while the Act specifically provides that the Administrator is responsible for costs in accordance with whatever judgment may be granted, it does not provide that the Administrator should be entitled to costs on the basis of the amounts claimed. The Plaintiffs in actions involving the Administrator must still prove their claims and it is the Administrator that requires them to do so in order to satisfy itself that it is responsible for payment of the judgment amount up to its limits. 37 Accordingly, the Administrator is entitled to its costs for the entire action taxed on a party and party basis under Column 3 of Schedule 3. 6. Party-Party Costs versus Solicitor-Client Costs The next issue to be resolved is whether costs should be awarded on a party-party basis or a solicitor-client basis. The general rule is set out in McCarthy v. Calgary R.C. Sep. Sch. Dist. No. 1 Bd. of Trustees, [1980] 5 W.W.R. 524 at 525 (Q.B.): … the general rule is that costs are awarded on a party-and-party basis against the unsuccessful litigant. An award of costs on this basis does not serve to completely indemnify the successful party but is viewed as a reasonable apportioning of the expense of the litigation between the parties. The rationale behind this rule is explained by Dubin J.A. in Foulis v. Robinson (1979), 21 O.R. (2d) 769 (C.A.): The expense of litigation is a matter of concern for all those interested in the administration of justice, but one must have regard for the burden which such costs place on all parties. Generally speaking, an award of costs on a party-and-party scale to the successful party strikes a proper balance as to the burden of costs which should be borne by the winner without putting litigation beyond the reach of the loser. There are, of course, cases in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs, but, in my respectful opinion, this is not such a case. Many courts have rejected attempts by counsel to have costs awarded on a solicitor-client basis, despite the general rule. Freedman J.A. in Evaskow v. Int. Brotherhood of Boilermakers, etc. (1969), 71 W.W.R. 565 at 570 (Man. C.A.), stated: Concerning costs I am bound to say that it must be a rare and most exceptional case in which costs will be awarded on a solicitor-and-client basis rather than on a party-and-party basis. And, Keith J. in Vanderclay Dev. Co. v. Inducon Engr. Ltd.; Vanderclay Dev. Co. v. Yorkland Dev. Ltd., [1969] 1 O.R. 41 (H.C.), stated: … one must be extremely cautious in departing from the general rule that costs awarded to a successful litigant are to be taxed as between party and party on the basis of an authoritative and well recognized tariff. If this principle were departed from, other than in exceptional cases, it is not difficult to visualize the indirect harm that could well be done by inhibiting prospective litigants from bringing to the attention of the Courts matters which they have every right to have put into litigation. At the same time the existence of the jurisdiction which I have already described does afford a real deterrent to persons who may be disposed to make wanton, scandalous and vicious charges against persons with whom they are in conflict. More recently, the Manitoba Court of Appeal in McDonald Dure Lumber Co. v. Marston Hldgs. Ltd., [1976] W.W.D. 80 … and Bjorninen v. Mercredi, [1984] 2 W.W.R. 646 … has affirmed the rule that solicitor-client costs should only be awarded in rare and exceptional circumstances. Cases that have awarded costs on a solicitor-client basis usually involved some form of misconduct or deception of the court, which clearly is not the situation before me. In McDonald Dure Lumber Co. v. Marston Hldgs. Ltd., [1976] W.W.D. 80 … and Bjorninen v. Mercredi, [1984] 2 W.W.R. 646 … has affirmed the rule that solicitor-client costs should only be awarded in rare and exceptional circumstances. Cases that have awarded costs on a solicitor-client basis usually involved some form of misconduct or deception of the court, which clearly is not the situation before me. In Cominco Ltd. v. Westinghouse Can. Ltd. (1980), 16 C.P.C. 19 at 22 (B.C. S.C.), Bouck J. comments that solicitor-client costs: … should only be made in circumstances where there has been scandalous conduct by the responsible party or some such exceptional incident …Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1987), 50 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 (Q.B.), at 5–7, per Wachowich J. 7. Scales of Costs There are three scales of costs. Alberta jurisprudence … recognizes three scales of costs: party-party, solicitor-client, solicitor and his own client… Research indicates that ambiguity with respect to the meaning and potential application of the “solicitor and his own client” scale to general litigation is not limited to Alberta. Lerner J., in Re Seitz (1974), 6 O.R. (2d) 460 (H.C.), at p. 465, interpreted the “solicitor and his own client” award as allowing those costs as would “provide complete indemnity to the client as to the costs essential to, and arising within, the four corners of litigation.” By identifying a scale of costs as “solicitor and his own client”, courts have invested that scale with application in litigation other than between a solicitor and his own client. The effect of the award of the scale as between general parties means only that the scale to be used is the scale that might be used by a solicitor against his resisting client. This concept has added significance in Alberta, where lawyers are entitled to act on a contingency basis. Thus, where the scale is “solicitor and his own client”, if the solicitor's contract with his own client is that he will be paid for his work at the rate of $300 per hour or on the basis of 35 per cent of the recovery, it is that fee which can be recovered against an unsuccessful defendant. All work requested to be done on a particular file and all work reasonably connected to the proceedings can be recovered on this scale. Because of the suggestion that the solicitor-client scale allows only the recover of reasonable fees, and because of the possibility that in specific cases “reasonable” will not be equivalent to “contractual”, I adopt, for the purposes of this decision, the meaning attributed by Lerner J. in Re Seitz to the term “solicitor and his own client”. Because of the confusion in the jurisprudence, I agree with the suggestion made by Megarry V.C. in EMI Records Ltd. v. Ian Cameron Wallace Ltd., [1983] Ch. 59 (Ch. D.), to the effect that when a judge wishes to indemnify a party in a costs award the phrase “indemnity basis” should be preferred to “solicitor and his own client”. Max Sonnenberg Inc. v. Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd. (1987), 48 Alta. L.R. (2d) 367 (Q.B.), at 370–71, per Veit J. And Agrios J. stated: There are three distinct scales of costs that may be awarded to a litigant. (1) party-and-party costs; (2) party-and-party costs on a solicitor-and-client basis; and (3) costs as between a solicitor and his own client. The first type is awarded in the majority of cases and is normally taxed in accordance with Sched. C. of the Rules of Court. The litigant is limited to the items enumerated there and only recovers a small part of his legal costs. The other two types of costs are awarded in special situations. “Party-and-party costs on a solicitor-and-client basis” refers to solicitor-and-client costs which are to be paid by the opposite party, while “costs as between a solicitor and his own client” refers to solicitor-client costs payable by the client himself. The distinction between the two is that between partial and total indemnification. In The Law of Costs (1968), Orkin [at p. 6] quotes Re Magee and Ottawa Sep. Sch. Bd., [1962] 32 D.L.R. (2d) 162 at 165–66 (Ont. H.C.): The distinction that is to be drawn between a case where the costs taxed on a solicitor and client basis are to be paid by an opposite party and one where they are to be paid by the client is this: if the client instructs the solicitor to do certain things or to take certain action, which is unnecessary for the proper presentation of the case, the client is liable to pay, providing the solicitor has properly safeguarded himself with full and fair advice. On the other hand, where the costs are to be paid by a third party, only those costs that are necessary for the proper presentation of the case may be recovered. This passage was adopted by D.C. McDonald J. of this court in Kalke v. 213156 Hldg. (1983), 47 A.R. 215 at 217, and was referred to by Stevenson D.C.J. (now of the Court of Appeal) in Vegreville & Dist. Savings & Credit Union v. Rurka (1978), 7 Alta. L.R. (2d) 390 at 391 (Dist. Ct.). Credit Foncier Trust Co. v. Hornigold (1984), 35 Alta. L.R. (2d) 341 at 344–45 ((Q.B.)). In Luft v. Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228, 2017 CarswellAlta 1183, 53 Alta. L.R. (6th) 44, Madam Justice Veldhuis said: 77 We would add the following comments about the distinction between solicitor and client costs and solicitor and own client costs, and the propriety of using the latter where the circumstances require more than the usual party and party costs based on Schedule C. The distinction between the two types of costs awards was discussed in Guarantee Co of North America v Beasse (1993), 139 AR 241, 1993 CarswellAlta 463 [cited to CarswellAlta]. Party and party costs assessed as between a “solicitor and client” include the reasonable fees and disbursements for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation. Costs between “solicitor and own client” allows for “frills or extras” authorized by the client, or which the client should reasonably pay his own solicitor, but which should not fairly be passed on to third parties who become responsible for those expenses. While the two methods of calculation might often result in the same amount, a third party litigant should not be required to pay for unnecessary extra services requested by a client. As pointed out in Trimac at paragraph 37, even in those rare cases where solicitor and client costs are justified: I do not take this to be a complete carte blanche so that a successful party can charge an unlimited amount. The contractual arrangement between the solicitor and client must be established and some check is necessary in order to justify the time spent and hourly rates which were presumably contracted for by Mr. Jackson. The key words are “essential to … and ‘arising within the four corners of litigation’”. 78 There is an important distinction between “solicitor and client costs” and “solicitor and own client costs”. An award of party and party costs calculated on a solicitor and client basis is rare and exceptional, but an award of solicitor and “own client” costs is virtually unheard of except where provided by contract. As the court noted in Guarantee Co of North America v Beasse at paragraphs 12–13: Turning to the issue of whether solicitor-and-own-client costs should ever be awarded in party-party litigation, I believe that the answer, for the reasons set out below, should be a loud “No”, except in the most exceptional, if any, cases … … I believe that any costs ever approved by a court should always be subject to the test of reasonableness, and necessity or prudence. Furthermore, in my view the court should never condone without examination, and, where questioned, without specific analysis and decision, costs that are arguably, or even potentially, unnecessary or unreasonable. In other words, I believe that an “unsuccessful” party should not be left to accept, without question, the costs incurred by a “successful” party, but rather a “successful” party, entitled, to solicitor-client costs, has a prima facie duty to demonstrate that they are reasonable, and necessary or prudent. Royal Trust Corp of Canada v Clarke (1989), 60 DLR (4th) 257 at 262–3, 35 BCLR (2d) 82 (CA) is to the same effect. In this case, no reasons were given for awarding solicitor and own client costs, and no proper justification could have been offered even if this was an appropriate case for solicitor and client costs. In Secure 2013 Group Inc. v. Tiger Calcium Services Inc., 2018 ABCA 110, 2018 CarswellAlta 1048, 68 Alta. L.R. (6th) 56, 18 C.P.C. (8th) 325, the court outlined four types of costs (the additional one being “lump sum costs”). The Court said: 12 Courts have broad discretion when awarding costs: Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, r 10.29–10.31. While different and sometimes inconsistent nomenclature is used, four types of costs are typically awarded: a. Party and party costs—determined in accordance with the tariff in Schedule C of the Rules and awarded in the majority of cases. They generally compensate the successful party for a portion of the legal fees incurred. The court may specify that the amount paid is a multiple, proportion or fraction of any of the amounts in the tariff: r 10.31(3). These costs are comparable to “ordinary costs” in British Columbia and to “partial indemnity costs” in Ontario: Mark M. Orkin, The Law of Costs (Aurora, Ont: Canada Law Book, 1987) (loose-leaf 2017 supplement), ch 1 at 3–4. b. Lump sum costs—fixed at a set amount: r 10.31(1)(b)(ii). c. Solicitor-client costs—provide full indemnity for all legal fees and disbursements reasonably incurred to the party to whom they are awarded. They are comparable to “special costs” in British Columbia and to “substantial indemnity” costs in Ontario: Orkin, ch 1 at 3–4. They are also called ‘solicitor and client costs’ or ‘party and party costs payable on a solicitor and client basis’. d. Solicitor and own client costs—allows a solicitor to recover from a client “frills or extras” authorized by the client which the client should reasonably pay its own solicitor, but which “should not fairly be passed on to third parties who become responsible for those expenses”: Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 at paras 77–78. When they exceed solicitor-client costs because they include services requested by a client that go beyond the reasonable fees and disbursements incurred for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation, such an award is only justified in the most exceptional circumstances. 8. When Schedule C Costs Result in Over Indemnification … there are situations under the new Schedule where there is the possibility of not merely full indemnification, but also an over indemnification above a litigant's actual legal costs. Party/party costs traditionally were meant to simply indemnify a party for the legal costs they had paid; they were not used to punish, penalize or benefit a party to the action. … When dealing with the issue of over indemnification in party/party costs it is necessary to point out that it is the final total of the costs award that is taken into account to determine if the costs are reasonable and whether there has been an over indemnification. … Traditionally it was commonly accepted that mere party/party costs should not exceed an amount that fully indemnifies a party for the actual costs they paid in advancing or defending an action. … In Alberta it is within the power of the taxation officer, under Rule 635, to reduce the party/party costs awarded under Schedule C to assure than an over indemnification does not occur. … It is my view, considering the above, that party/party costs where there has been a formal offer of settlement under the Rules of Court should be taxed based on the tariff amounts as set under Schedule C and as outlined in Rule 174, notwithstanding that [an] over indemnification may occur. This would promote settlement by punishing those who refuse reasonable offers. Furthermore, it would provide an even playing field irrespective of the actual cost of the lawyer, or the fact that a party is represented through legal aid or self represented. … … absent a direction from the court to the contrary, the taxing officer should only allow an over indemnification where the Rules with respect to an offer of settlement apply. Absent such an offer, or direction to the contrary from the court, the standard principle that party/party costs merely provides indemnification for the parties actual legal costs should apply. Shillingford v. Dalbridge Group Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 361 (Q.B.), at 366–369, per Perras, J. In MacLeod v. MacLeod (2001), 287 A.R. 43 (Master), Master Alberstat applied the Shillingford v. Dalbridge Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 28, 2000 CarswellAlta 48, 268 A.R. 324, 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 361, case in awarding costs when the successful party was represented by Calgary Legal Guidance which was an agency that charged clients only a nominal fee and disbursements. See also the digest of RVB Managements Ltd. v. Rocky Mountain House (Town), 2015 ABCA 304 under the heading of “Multiplier”. 9. Costs as Indemnity Rule 10.31 authorizes costs on an indemnity basis. The second issue is whether, as between litigants other than a solicitor suing his own client for fees, there is authority to award costs to a successful party on an indemnity basis. I am of the view that R. 601(1) provides that authority and that nothing in RR. 613–626 derogates from it. Solicitor-Client Costs and the Workers' Compensation Board In Nabors Canada LP v. Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board, Appeals Commission) (2005), 51 Alta. L.R. (4th) 343 (Q.B.); affirmed (2006) 66 Alta. L.R. (4th) 199 (C.A.), the widow of a worker killed while engaged in his employment duties had successfully made a claim against the Workers' Compensation Board. The employer appealed that determination, and the Board successfully applied to be added to the appeal. Ultimately, the widow succeeded in the appeal, and sought solicitor-client costs. In granting those costs, Sulyma J. reviewed the general rule of party-party costs, but concluded that the general rule should not apply when a worker (or someone claiming through a worker) is successful against the W.C.B. Her Ladyship said, at pp. 350–352: The law indicates that, absent exceptional circumstances, the successful party is entitled to party and party costs. Although this issue remains one of discretion, discretion must be consistent with established principles and practice. This case did not involve a trial. However, it did involve an appeal of an administrative decision. The Appellant Nabors had a statutory right of appeal. The W.C.B. had an interest in the appeal since the decision appealed from overturned its decision. Certainly the issues were not frivolous or vexatious, since they arose as a result of recent legislative changes and decisions of this Court. With respect to the Appellant Nabors, I cannot find that simply as a result of its being a wealthy party it ought to pay higher costs. I agree with Nabors' submission that the question of whether a party can afford costs is separate and distinct from whether the party opposite is entitled to such an award. In so finding, I do have regard to the obvious difference in the financial situation of the Respondent widow and a large and profitable corporation. However, Sitler also argues that the intended nature of the workers' compensation scheme renders this an exceptional circumstances. As noted by the Supreme Court in Pasiechnyk at para. 26: The importance of the historic trade-off has been recognized by the courts. In Reference re Validity of Sections 32 and 34 of the Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (1987), 44 D.L.R. (4th) 501 (Nfld. C.A.), Goodridge C.J. compared the advantages of workers' compensation against its principal disadvantage: benefits that are paid immediately, whether or not the employer is solvent, and without the costs and uncertainties inherent in the tort system; however, there may be some who would recover more from a tort action than they would under the Act. (Emphasis added) But, as a result of Nabors' appeal, Sitler has not received the advantage of either immediate benefits or certainty. Moreover, if she is awarded only party and party costs, she loses the other intended benefit of avoiding the tort system—the avoidance of litigation costs. Nabors commenced this appeal; Sitler had no choice but to respond or lose the compensation to which she and her children were entitled. Full indemnification of her costs are necessary in this case for justice to be done. This is not to suggest that Nabors conducted the litigation in any improper manner, but if the historic trade-off is to continue to provide the advantages intended in return for the possible benefits foregone, litigation expenses should not become a potential bar to successful W.C.B. claimants. … In my view improved access to court review would be illusory if deserving claimants are denied full indemnity for their costs when employers appeal to a court. Further, the rationale underlying the general rule regarding party and party costs is directly related to the allocation of costs and risk in the tort system; to apply the rule in a system that is expressly intended to be an alternative to the tort system is illogical. I do, however, view the position of the W.C.B. somewhat differently than that of Nabors. While I find that Nabors' conduct of the litigation was not inappropriate, I agree with the Respondent's submission that the W.C.B. took contrary positions before this Court in a very short time period and could be said to have re-litigated its position in regards to the standard of review. Indeed, I am at a loss to reconcile the differing positions. I cannot do so on the basis that the functional and pragmatic approach dictates that each case must be analyzed on its merits. I find that the functional and pragmatic approach would in most instances, and certainly in this case, result in the W.C.B. taking a consistent position towards the standard of review. I say this despite the fact that the analysis of the standard of review must consider the nature of the issue. In this regard I agree with Sitler's submission that the nature of the issue before the tribunal was exactly the same as that which was before Madam Justice Moreau in Buettner. I recognize that the W.C.B. is entitled to explore the scope of the standard of review, but the cost of that exploration was not intended to be borne by injured workers, their widows, and children—the intended beneficiaries of the system. Therefore, the position of the W.C.B. has been abusive, has resulted in attempted re-litigation, and frankly does not serve this party well in its various appearances before the Court. On this basis there is an exceptional circumstance justifying an increased level of costs, and justice is served by such an award. I award solicitor-client costs to the Respondent to be shared equally by both the W.C.B. and Nabors. 17. Costs Associated With Changing Counsel In McAteer v.
