That is, the circumstances rather than a presumption supported the costs award for consent orders. [30] In ASC (AB) Facility Inc v Man-Shield (Alta) Construction, 2018 ABQB 855, Justice Antonio, as she then was, commented on Waterous Investments at paras 19 and 20 as follows: [19] It may be possible to debate whether awarding costs for consent orders against one consenting party would encourage or discourage compromise. In any event, I am unable to read this passage as creating a rule that the party with ultimate success must receive costs for consent orders absent any prior costs award. There may be circumstances of contention in which hard work was done on one or both sides to reach consent. There may be other circumstances in which a consent order was reached with little effort, for instance on a pro forma procedural matter. [20] Absent a fact-specific reason to do so, I am not persuaded that the costs paradigm of “spoils to the victor” should be applied to consent orders. Therefore this portion of ASC's costs claim is dismissed. When Waterous Investments is read in context, Justice Antonio's approach is similar to Justice Veit's. A cost award for even a consent order may be appropriate if “hard work” was necessary to obtain the order or there was some other “fact-specific reason” to award costs for the order.
paragraphs.heading: Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions

sentences.text: The primary purpose of a costs award is to partly indemnify the successful party for the costs of the litigation: British Columbia (Minister of Forests) v.
Okanagan Indian Band, 2003 SCC 71 at paras.
Since a self-represented litigant does not incur any legal fees, the ordinary objective of indemnification is not achieved.

Costs awards do, however, achieve other purposes: they can be used to encourage settlement, or to prevent frivolous, vexatious or harassing litigation, and they can also be used to encourage economy and efficiency during litigation.
Rule 10.31(5) ensures that those purposes of a costs award can be achieved even where a party is self-represented.
9 Previous decisions have observed that awarding costs to self-represented litigants raises difficult policy issues.

The expectation that costs might be received can actually invert the usual objectives of costs, by encouraging litigation and discouraging settlement “because of an anticipated windfall to the unrepresented litigant that could result from a costs award”: Dechant v.
Law Society of Alberta, 2001 ABCA 81 at para.
As Dechant observed at paras.
16–7, self-represented litigants do not necessarily bear a greater personal burden: 16 It is true that unrepresented litigants expend time and effort presenting their law suits.
Represented litigants, however, also sacrifice a considerable amount of their own time and effort for which no compensation is paid.
Any award of costs is merely a partial reimbursement for their lawyer's fees.
As noted, an award of costs to represented litigants should never be higher than their solicitor-client fees, which are only awarded in exceptional circumstances.

Thus, applying an identical costs schedule to both represented and unrepresented litigants will work an inequity against the represented litigant who, even with an award of costs, will be left with some legal fees to pay and no compensation for a personal investment of time.
What the Rules do provide is that both kinds of litigants are to be paid for their out-of-pocket expenses.

17 … Applying an identical costs schedule to the unrepresented litigants, who have no out-of-pocket expenses for the legal fee portion of the suit, effectively awards fees for their own time and work.
In short, self-litigation could become an occupation.
For these reasons, a self-represented litigant should generally not receive costs unless that would serve one of the policy reasons for which costs awards are made.
10 The appellant Simonson suggests he should receive two-thirds of the assessable costs during the time he was self-represented.
Such an award, however, would still represent an indemnity for expenses that were never incurred.
While it is undoubtedly true that Simonson took time away from his business affairs to attend the trial, that is true of most litigants, whether they are self-represented or not.

There is no evidence on this record that Simonson exercised any special skill during the trial (such as briefing the law, or arguing complex issues), nor that he was burdened more than the average litigant.
In the circumstances, it is appropriate that for the portion of the trial when he was self-represented he only receive assessable disbursements.
In Melanson v.
Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board Appeals Commission), 2011 ABQB 367, 511 A.R.
178, 2011 CarswellAlta 2516, 64 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 192, Justice Lee concluded that in the action before him the Workers' Compensation Board was a party under R.
He then commented (at paragraph 25) on R.
10.31(5): 25 I agree with the depiction of a self-represented litigant offered by the WCB as accurate.
I am of the view that Rule 10.31(5) of the Rules of Court contemplates individual persons who are parties to an action and represent themselves without the services of legal counsel.
In this action, both the WCB and the Appeals Commission as creatures of statute, were represented by legal counsel: see, WCA, ss.

It will constitute an unjustifiable stretch of the term if a creature of statute provided with services of legal counsel on judicial appeal before the court is construed as a self represented litigant.
The following cases were decided before R.
10.31(5) came into being, and show that even then unrepresented litigants were sometimes awarded costs.
It is clear that the Court of Queen's Bench in Alberta recognizes the granting of costs to unrepresented litigants.
I agree with and I adopt the reasoning of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Skidmore v.
Blackmore[(1995), 122 D.L.R.

(4th) 330]… The awarding of costs in this province, as in British Columbia, is discretionary … Furthermore, it is clear from the Rules of Court that the reasons for awarding costs are beyond mere indemnification.
Rule 601(1) and Rule 174 show that costs also exist to encourage settlement and discourage misconduct on the part of litigants.
Thus, I find that the Applicant is entitled to costs in this case despite the fact that she was unrepresented by counsel some of the time.
C.
C.
L.R.
(3d) 300 (Q.B.), at 306–307, per Marceau J.
In Edmonton (Police Service) v.

Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2019 ABQB 864, 2019 CarswellAlta 2434, Justice Graesser said: [30] In summary, I note that in Alberta, nothing has really changed since my decision in LL v GB, 2009 ABQB 322, which was decided before the 2010 Rules of Court changes.
The approach has not changed with the new Rules of Court, and the Alberta courts have not followed along the Ontario or British Columbia lines.
I said in LL at paragraph 67: [67] I think the following principles are applicable to the award of costs in favour of a successful self-represented litigant: 1.
There is no automatic rule entitling a self-represented litigant to costs.

While there is a presumption in favour of awarding costs on a party and party basis to a successful represented litigant, a self-represented litigant bears a stronger onus of establishing an entitlement to costs; 2.
In determining entitlement, the Court should have regard to the factors set out in Dechant; 3.

To achieve fairness, a self-represented party's time is a minor factor in the consideration of costs, and then only to the extent that the self-represented party has spent more time on the matter than one would expect a represented party to have spent.
The Court's discretion should be exercised after an analysis of the Dechant factors; 5.
Only after the Court has exercised its discretion in favour of awarding costs to a self-represented litigant should the Court determine the quantum of costs; 6.
Schedule C is a guide to determining quantum, but the Court may exercise a discretion to award a lump sum, or all or a portion of Schedule C costs; and 7.
The Court should try to avoid turning the assessment of costs into a further trial.
[31] I will offer a few further observations: 1.

It would be very rare for costs in favour of a self-represented litigant to exceed the amount of costs that would be awarded to a represented party in the same case; in other words, if Schedule C column 1 would normally be appropriate, the self-represented litigant should not receive more than that even if his or her lost opportunity costs exceeded that amount; 2.

It is difficult if not impossible to reconcile the principles in Dechant and Hogarth with a self-represented litigant being awarded double costs under Rule 4.29, or enhanced costs unless the self-represented litigant can demonstrate that such amounts are still within what the litigant can prove on balance is within his or her lost opportunity; 3.

Issues such having been taken unfair advantage of procedurally or misconduct by the other party during the litigation (such as those things usually advanced by parties seeking solicitor and client costs or enhanced costs) may justify in appropriate circumstances some measure of punitive cost award in favour of a self-represented litigant.

I think there is a clear distinction to be made between litigation initiated by a self-represented litigant or maintained by the litigant him or herself after counsel has withdrawn for whatever reason, and a litigant responding to litigation brought against him or her.
It seems to me that there is less worry about a litigant turning the litigation into an occupation when the self-represented litigant is the defendant or respondent.
The litigant may have little choice but to represent him or herself for financial reasons.
Legal aid is rarely available for civil litigants outside the family law area, and even in that area is limited to very poor litigants.
A sued person has no choice but to respond, and faces a system where his or her legal costs will be fully indemnified on success only in very exceptional circumstances.
Costs for Intervenors In Auer v.
Auer, 2021 ABQB 860, 2021 CarswellAlta 2720, Mr.
Auer unsuccessfully challenged the jurisdictional foundation of the Federal Child Support Guidelines.
The Attorney General of Canada was an Intervenor in those proceedings and sought costs against Mr.
Auer.
Justice Rothwell discussed when costs should be awarded to an Intervenor: [13] Mr.
Auer cites the decision of Stoney Tribal Council v PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd, 2000 ABCA 164 at para 2 [Stoney Tribal Council] for the proposition that intervenors are generally not entitled to costs.
In that case Chevron Canada Resources (Chevron) was granted intervenor status to respond to a constitutional issue raised by the Stoney Tribal Council.
The Stoney Tribal Council withdrew its constitutional challenge and Chevron did not participate in the appeal.
The Court declined to grant Chevron its intervention costs.

[14] The AGC cited Lynnview Ridge Residents' Action Committee v Imperial Oil Limited, 2005 ABCA 375 [Lynnview] and Canadian Union of Postal Workers v Her Majesty in Right of Canada, 2017 ONSC 6503 [CUPW] in support of the proposition that costs, in appropriate circumstances, may be awarded to intervenors.
[15] Intervenors are generally granted intervenor status to offer an argument that is useful and different and/or to assist the Court.
They generally take the record as they find it and their participation is limited: Suncor Energy Inc v Unifor, Local 707 A, 2014 ABQB 555.

[16] In Lynnview the Alberta Court of Appeal noted the following considerations with respect to the appropriateness of awarding costs to an intervenor, at para 25: I conclude that there are circumstances where an intervener with a special interest should be awarded costs.

Although the circumstances will vary, the factors to be taken into account in determining whether it is appropriate to deviate from the general rule include: • Has the intervener contributed to the court's deliberations by adding a viewpoint that otherwise would not have been considered?

Alternatively, did the parties themselves present the same arguments or points of view? • Is there legislation relevant to the case to suggest whether the intervener has a special interest or an important role to play? • What is the nature of the intervener's special interest?
The interest might be financial, proprietary, non-pecuniary or other.
[17] The Ontario Court of Superior Justice in CUPW identified six factors for consideration in its decision, at para 31: i.
What is the nature and extent of the intervener's interest in the issues that were before the court and in the outcome of the proceeding? ii.
What was the nature and extent of the intervener's involvement in the proceeding? iii.
What are the intervener's resources? iv.
Was the intervener successful on the merits? v.
Did one of the parties anticipate or provoke the intervener's involvement? vi.
Did the terms of the order granting leave to intervene address the possibility of a cost award?
[18] I note that there are similarities between the Lynnview and CUPW factors but I will focus primarily on the Lynnview factors as they emanate from the Court of Appeal of Alberta.
In the end, costs were awarded to the Attorney General on Column 2 of Schedule C.
Number of Bills of Costs when Multiple Defendants In Kucher v.
Seaboard Life Assurance Co.

1 (Q.B.), the plaintiff provided two bills of costs: one in each of two actions tried together and commenced by it in respect of two insurance policies (one issued by Seaboard and one issued by CIBC).
Clarke J., at p.

7, said: It was the plaintiff's position that they had to fight both actions, both CIBC and Seaboard had counsel and both counsel participated in the defence of the claim, so it was appropriate to award separate costs against each of those parties as represented by the separate bills of costs… I have concluded that where there are items of costs such as commencing proceedings by Statement of Claim which are clearly individual to each of the defendants a bill of costs is appropriate for each defendant.

On the other hand, where actions were undertaken for the benefit of all of the defendants and it was agreed that the activity could be used by all of the defendants then those costs should be prorated amongst the defendants involved.
Dealing more specifically with the trial, I am satisfied that there should be one bill of costs for the actvities at trial.
The defendants presented their case as a common case and there was no significant overlap in any of the actions taken by the counsel for each of the defendants.
Schedule C and Appeals from Provincial Court In Yi v.
Varadi (c.o.b.
Key Homes Inspections), 2013 ABQB 441, 2013 CarswellAlta 1508, 560 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 415, Justice Lee held that Schedule C applies to appeals from Provincial Court to the Court of Queen's Bench.
In his reasons, his Lordship acknowledged that there is a disagreement on the topic amongst his judicial colleagues.

He said, at paragraph 9: 9 I conclude that the Schedule C costs are still appropriate and applicable for an appeal of a Provincial Court Decision to the Court of Queen's Bench, notwithstanding that there is no specific provision for this in Schedule C.
Although my colleague Veit, J. generally disagreed with this proposition in Condominium Plan 8022962 v.
Malinowsky, 2005 ABQB 346, and Mahar v.

Edmonton Dream Cleaners Ltd, 2005 ABQB 37, I conclude that the quantum of Schedule C column 1 costs are relatively modest, and the categories provided for in Schedule C for an appeal are generally equally applicable to appeals to the Court of Queen's Bench from the Provincial Court.

Specifically I conclude that the Schedule C costs are appropriate for an appeal of a Provincial Court Decision to the Court of Queen's Bench in the current matter given it's (sic) complexity and issues of law.
Justice Pentelechuk said, in Genge v.
Centron Residential Corp., 2014 ABQB 50, 2014 CarswellAlta 270, at paragraph 27: …Yi v.

Varadi, 2013 ABQB 441, at para 9, provides authority for the award of Schedule C costs for an Appeal of a Provincial Court decision to the Court of Queen's Bench, notwithstanding that there is no specific provision for this in Schedule C. . . . . .
Costs and the Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act In Ezzedine v.
Dalgard (2007), 73 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 58 (Alta.
Q.B.), the Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act was included as a defendant in a motor vehicle accident action because the uninsured defendant Dalgard had been noted in default.
At the end of the trial, Mackin J. ruled that the Administrator was entitled to costs.
The Administrator sought costs based on the amounts claimed (Column 5) as opposed to the Administrator's statutorily set monetary exposure (Column 3).
The learned trial judge held that the Administrator was only entitled to Column 3 costs.
Macklin J. said, at p.
68: 35 In my view, the Administrator is only entitled to those costs that reflect its actual exposure in the case.
It is conceded that the Administrator's maximum total exposure, regardless of the amounts that might be awarded to the Plaintiffs, is $200,000.

While the Statements of Claim seek damages exceeding the limits of the Administrator's exposure, all parties were fully aware at all times that the Administrator would never be responsible for any payment of damages exceeding the prescribed limit.

36 The difference between the Administrator as a Defendant and other Defendants who would be entitled to have their costs determined against the Plaintiff on the basis of the amount claimed is that other Defendants' exposure is not limited as is that of the Administrator.

Further, while the Act specifically provides that the Administrator is responsible for costs in accordance with whatever judgment may be granted, it does not provide that the Administrator should be entitled to costs on the basis of the amounts claimed.

The Plaintiffs in actions involving the Administrator must still prove their claims and it is the Administrator that requires them to do so in order to satisfy itself that it is responsible for payment of the judgment amount up to its limits.
37 Accordingly, the Administrator is entitled to its costs for the entire action taxed on a party and party basis under Column 3 of Schedule 3.
Party-Party Costs versus Solicitor-Client Costs The next issue to be resolved is whether costs should be awarded on a party-party basis or a solicitor-client basis.
The general rule is set out in McCarthy v.
Calgary R.C.
Sep.
Sch.
Dist.
No.
1 Bd. of Trustees, [1980] 5 W.W.R.
524 at 525 (Q.B.): … the general rule is that costs are awarded on a party-and-party basis against the unsuccessful litigant.
An award of costs on this basis does not serve to completely indemnify the successful party but is viewed as a reasonable apportioning of the expense of the litigation between the parties.
The rationale behind this rule is explained by Dubin J.A. in Foulis v.
Robinson (1979), 21 O.R.

(2d) 769 (C.A.): The expense of litigation is a matter of concern for all those interested in the administration of justice, but one must have regard for the burden which such costs place on all parties.

Generally speaking, an award of costs on a party-and-party scale to the successful party strikes a proper balance as to the burden of costs which should be borne by the winner without putting litigation beyond the reach of the loser.
There are, of course, cases in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs, but, in my respectful opinion, this is not such a case.
Many courts have rejected attempts by counsel to have costs awarded on a solicitor-client basis, despite the general rule.
Freedman J.A. in Evaskow v.
Int.
Brotherhood of Boilermakers, etc.

C.A.), stated: Concerning costs I am bound to say that it must be a rare and most exceptional case in which costs will be awarded on a solicitor-and-client basis rather than on a party-and-party basis.
And, Keith J. in Vanderclay Dev.
Co. v.
Inducon Engr.
Ltd.; Vanderclay Dev.
Co. v.
Yorkland Dev.

41 (H.C.), stated: … one must be extremely cautious in departing from the general rule that costs awarded to a successful litigant are to be taxed as between party and party on the basis of an authoritative and well recognized tariff.

If this principle were departed from, other than in exceptional cases, it is not difficult to visualize the indirect harm that could well be done by inhibiting prospective litigants from bringing to the attention of the Courts matters which they have every right to have put into litigation.

At the same time the existence of the jurisdiction which I have already described does afford a real deterrent to persons who may be disposed to make wanton, scandalous and vicious charges against persons with whom they are in conflict.
More recently, the Manitoba Court of Appeal in McDonald Dure Lumber Co. v.
Marston Hldgs.
80 … and Bjorninen v.
Mercredi, [1984] 2 W.W.R.
646 … has affirmed the rule that solicitor-client costs should only be awarded in rare and exceptional circumstances.
Cases that have awarded costs on a solicitor-client basis usually involved some form of misconduct or deception of the court, which clearly is not the situation before me.
In McDonald Dure Lumber Co. v.
Marston Hldgs.
80 … and Bjorninen v.
Mercredi, [1984] 2 W.W.R.
646 … has affirmed the rule that solicitor-client costs should only be awarded in rare and exceptional circumstances.
Cases that have awarded costs on a solicitor-client basis usually involved some form of misconduct or deception of the court, which clearly is not the situation before me.
In Cominco Ltd. v.
Westinghouse Can.
Ltd.

S.C.), Bouck J. comments that solicitor-client costs: … should only be made in circumstances where there has been scandalous conduct by the responsible party or some such exceptional incident …Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v.
Canadian Commercial Bank (1987), 50 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 1 (Q.B.), at 5–7, per Wachowich J.
Scales of Costs There are three scales of costs.

Alberta jurisprudence … recognizes three scales of costs: party-party, solicitor-client, solicitor and his own client… Research indicates that ambiguity with respect to the meaning and potential application of the “solicitor and his own client” scale to general litigation is not limited to Alberta.
Lerner J., in Re Seitz (1974), 6 O.R.

465, interpreted the “solicitor and his own client” award as allowing those costs as would “provide complete indemnity to the client as to the costs essential to, and arising within, the four corners of litigation.” By identifying a scale of costs as “solicitor and his own client”, courts have invested that scale with application in litigation other than between a solicitor and his own client.
The effect of the award of the scale as between general parties means only that the scale to be used is the scale that might be used by a solicitor against his resisting client.
This concept has added significance in Alberta, where lawyers are entitled to act on a contingency basis.

Thus, where the scale is “solicitor and his own client”, if the solicitor's contract with his own client is that he will be paid for his work at the rate of $300 per hour or on the basis of 35 per cent of the recovery, it is that fee which can be recovered against an unsuccessful defendant.
All work requested to be done on a particular file and all work reasonably connected to the proceedings can be recovered on this scale.

Because of the suggestion that the solicitor-client scale allows only the recover of reasonable fees, and because of the possibility that in specific cases “reasonable” will not be equivalent to “contractual”, I adopt, for the purposes of this decision, the meaning attributed by Lerner J. in Re Seitz to the term “solicitor and his own client”.
Because of the confusion in the jurisprudence, I agree with the suggestion made by Megarry V.C. in EMI Records Ltd. v.
Ian Cameron Wallace Ltd., [1983] Ch.
D.), to the effect that when a judge wishes to indemnify a party in a costs award the phrase “indemnity basis” should be preferred to “solicitor and his own client”.
Max Sonnenberg Inc. v.
Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd.
L.R.
(2d) 367 (Q.B.), at 370–71, per Veit J.
And Agrios J. stated: There are three distinct scales of costs that may be awarded to a litigant.
(1) party-and-party costs; (2) party-and-party costs on a solicitor-and-client basis; and (3) costs as between a solicitor and his own client.
The first type is awarded in the majority of cases and is normally taxed in accordance with Sched.
C. of the Rules of Court.
The litigant is limited to the items enumerated there and only recovers a small part of his legal costs.

The other two types of costs are awarded in special situations. “Party-and-party costs on a solicitor-and-client basis” refers to solicitor-and-client costs which are to be paid by the opposite party, while “costs as between a solicitor and his own client” refers to solicitor-client costs payable by the client himself.
The distinction between the two is that between partial and total indemnification.
In The Law of Costs (1968), Orkin [at p.
6] quotes Re Magee and Ottawa Sep.
Sch.

H.C.): The distinction that is to be drawn between a case where the costs taxed on a solicitor and client basis are to be paid by an opposite party and one where they are to be paid by the client is this: if the client instructs the solicitor to do certain things or to take certain action, which is unnecessary for the proper presentation of the case, the client is liable to pay, providing the solicitor has properly safeguarded himself with full and fair advice.
On the other hand, where the costs are to be paid by a third party, only those costs that are necessary for the proper presentation of the case may be recovered.
This passage was adopted by D.C.
McDonald J. of this court in Kalke v.
215 at 217, and was referred to by Stevenson D.C.J.
(now of the Court of Appeal) in Vegreville & Dist.
Savings & Credit Union v.
Rurka (1978), 7 Alta.
L.R.
Ct.).
Credit Foncier Trust Co. v.
Hornigold (1984), 35 Alta.
L.R.
In Luft v.
Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228, 2017 CarswellAlta 1183, 53 Alta.
L.R.

(6th) 44, Madam Justice Veldhuis said: 77 We would add the following comments about the distinction between solicitor and client costs and solicitor and own client costs, and the propriety of using the latter where the circumstances require more than the usual party and party costs based on Schedule C.
The distinction between the two types of costs awards was discussed in Guarantee Co of North America v Beasse (1993), 139 AR 241, 1993 CarswellAlta 463 [cited to CarswellAlta].
Party and party costs assessed as between a “solicitor and client” include the reasonable fees and disbursements for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation.

Costs between “solicitor and own client” allows for “frills or extras” authorized by the client, or which the client should reasonably pay his own solicitor, but which should not fairly be passed on to third parties who become responsible for those expenses.
While the two methods of calculation might often result in the same amount, a third party litigant should not be required to pay for unnecessary extra services requested by a client.

As pointed out in Trimac at paragraph 37, even in those rare cases where solicitor and client costs are justified: I do not take this to be a complete carte blanche so that a successful party can charge an unlimited amount.

The contractual arrangement between the solicitor and client must be established and some check is necessary in order to justify the time spent and hourly rates which were presumably contracted for by Mr.
Jackson.
The key words are “essential to … and ‘arising within the four corners of litigation’”.
78 There is an important distinction between “solicitor and client costs” and “solicitor and own client costs”.

An award of party and party costs calculated on a solicitor and client basis is rare and exceptional, but an award of solicitor and “own client” costs is virtually unheard of except where provided by contract.

As the court noted in Guarantee Co of North America v Beasse at paragraphs 12–13: Turning to the issue of whether solicitor-and-own-client costs should ever be awarded in party-party litigation, I believe that the answer, for the reasons set out below, should be a loud “No”, except in the most exceptional, if any, cases … … I believe that any costs ever approved by a court should always be subject to the test of reasonableness, and necessity or prudence.

Furthermore, in my view the court should never condone without examination, and, where questioned, without specific analysis and decision, costs that are arguably, or even potentially, unnecessary or unreasonable.

In other words, I believe that an “unsuccessful” party should not be left to accept, without question, the costs incurred by a “successful” party, but rather a “successful” party, entitled, to solicitor-client costs, has a prima facie duty to demonstrate that they are reasonable, and necessary or prudent.
Royal Trust Corp of Canada v Clarke (1989), 60 DLR (4th) 257 at 262–3, 35 BCLR (2d) 82 (CA) is to the same effect.

In this case, no reasons were given for awarding solicitor and own client costs, and no proper justification could have been offered even if this was an appropriate case for solicitor and client costs.
In Secure 2013 Group Inc. v.
Tiger Calcium Services Inc., 2018 ABCA 110, 2018 CarswellAlta 1048, 68 Alta.
L.R.
(8th) 325, the court outlined four types of costs (the additional one being “lump sum costs”).
The Court said: 12 Courts have broad discretion when awarding costs: Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, r 10.29–10.31.
While different and sometimes inconsistent nomenclature is used, four types of costs are typically awarded: a.
Party and party costs—determined in accordance with the tariff in Schedule C of the Rules and awarded in the majority of cases.
They generally compensate the successful party for a portion of the legal fees incurred.
The court may specify that the amount paid is a multiple, proportion or fraction of any of the amounts in the tariff: r 10.31(3).
These costs are comparable to “ordinary costs” in British Columbia and to “partial indemnity costs” in Ontario: Mark M.
Orkin, The Law of Costs (Aurora, Ont: Canada Law Book, 1987) (loose-leaf 2017 supplement), ch 1 at 3–4. b.
Lump sum costs—fixed at a set amount: r 10.31(1)(b)(ii). c.
Solicitor-client costs—provide full indemnity for all legal fees and disbursements reasonably incurred to the party to whom they are awarded.
They are comparable to “special costs” in British Columbia and to “substantial indemnity” costs in Ontario: Orkin, ch 1 at 3–4.
They are also called ‘solicitor and client costs’ or ‘party and party costs payable on a solicitor and client basis’. d.

Solicitor and own client costs—allows a solicitor to recover from a client “frills or extras” authorized by the client which the client should reasonably pay its own solicitor, but which “should not fairly be passed on to third parties who become responsible for those expenses”: Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 at paras 77–78.

When they exceed solicitor-client costs because they include services requested by a client that go beyond the reasonable fees and disbursements incurred for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation, such an award is only justified in the most exceptional circumstances.

When Schedule C Costs Result in Over Indemnification … there are situations under the new Schedule where there is the possibility of not merely full indemnification, but also an over indemnification above a litigant's actual legal costs.

Party/party costs traditionally were meant to simply indemnify a party for the legal costs they had paid; they were not used to punish, penalize or benefit a party to the action. … When dealing with the issue of over indemnification in party/party costs it is necessary to point out that it is the final total of the costs award that is taken into account to determine if the costs are reasonable and whether there has been an over indemnification. … Traditionally it was commonly accepted that mere party/party costs should not exceed an amount that fully indemnifies a party for the actual costs they paid in advancing or defending an action. … In Alberta it is within the power of the taxation officer, under Rule 635, to reduce the party/party costs awarded under Schedule C to assure than an over indemnification does not occur. … It is my view, considering the above, that party/party costs where there has been a formal offer of settlement under the Rules of Court should be taxed based on the tariff amounts as set under Schedule C and as outlined in Rule 174, notwithstanding that [an] over indemnification may occur.
This would promote settlement by punishing those who refuse reasonable offers.

Furthermore, it would provide an even playing field irrespective of the actual cost of the lawyer, or the fact that a party is represented through legal aid or self represented. … … absent a direction from the court to the contrary, the taxing officer should only allow an over indemnification where the Rules with respect to an offer of settlement apply.
Absent such an offer, or direction to the contrary from the court, the standard principle that party/party costs merely provides indemnification for the parties actual legal costs should apply.
Shillingford v.
Dalbridge Group Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 361 (Q.B.), at 366–369, per Perras, J.
In MacLeod v.
MacLeod (2001), 287 A.R.
43 (Master), Master Alberstat applied the Shillingford v.
Dalbridge Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 28, 2000 CarswellAlta 48, 268 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 361, case in awarding costs when the successful party was represented by Calgary Legal Guidance which was an agency that charged clients only a nominal fee and disbursements.
See also the digest of RVB Managements Ltd. v.
Rocky Mountain House (Town), 2015 ABCA 304 under the heading of “Multiplier”.
Costs as Indemnity Rule 10.31 authorizes costs on an indemnity basis.
The second issue is whether, as between litigants other than a solicitor suing his own client for fees, there is authority to award costs to a successful party on an indemnity basis.
I am of the view that R.

Challenges to the integrity of counsel must also be noted.
Counsel are officers of the court and play an important role in the delivery of justice.

An unjustifiable attack on judges and legal counsel imperils the judicial system's capacity to fairly try disputes.141 126 On these occasions, courts order the party responsible for blameworthy conduct to pay the payee an amount that is intended to reduce the victorious party's out-of-pocket legal costs to close to zero or relieve the unsuccessful party of costs obligations.142 While orders of this nature express the court's strong disapproval of the payor's conduct, they should not be regarded as penal in nature.
They simply make the payee whole in one limited respect—the pocketbook.
In Sidorsky v.
CFCN Communications Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 255 (C.A.); [reconsideration refused (1998), 216 A.R.
151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999), 232 A.R.
189 (C.A.)], the Court of Appeal, at p.
264, specifically referred to the nine factors set out by Hutchinson J. in Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.
At p.
266 of Sidorsky, the Court of Appeal again quoted Hutchinson J. in respect of the “two major propositions mitigating [sic] against an award of solicitor-client costs.” In Morrison Petroleums Ltd. v.
Phoenix Canada Oil Co.
L.R.
Justice Moshansky said, at p.
218, “that the 9 factors outlined [in Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 403] apply equally to either a plaintiff or a defendant.” His Lordship went on to say, at p.

219: … that when considering the awarding of costs on an indemnity basis the Court must make a careful analysis of the facts in each case to determine whether or not such an award is appropriate, the trial judge having had the benefit of seeing and hearing the witnesses and distilling the essence of the lawsuit.
In Fitzpatrick v.
Industrial Incomes Ltd.
139 (Q.B.), Waite J. granted an application for solicitor-client costs in the amount of $89,000, relying upon Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 403 (Q.B.), and in particular item 5 in Hutchinson J.'s reasons (as quoted above).
At p.

141, Waite J. said: The primary principle upon which this judgment in costs is based is that when the litigant against whom costs are to be assessed has been guilty of positive misconduct in the litigation process, the scale of costs should be such as to act as a deterrent to others.
This is the punitive element in costs whereby a court expresses its disapproval of the conduct of the litigant.
In Schwartz v.
Longview Motel & Saloon Corp.
L.R.
Hunt J. applied Jackson v.
Trimac at p.
384, and went on to say that a higher standard applies to lawyers when determining whether solicitor-client costs ought to be awarded in cases of breach of fiduciary duty.
At pp.
384–85 Her Ladyship said: Certain of the authorities suggest that courts are reluctant to award solicitor-client costs on breaches of fiduciary duty of professionals other than lawyers.
Per Veit J. in Max Sonnenberg Inc. v.
Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd.
L.R.
This implies that a higher standard ought to apply to lawyers, and I agree.
In Osborne v.
Justice Marshall noted that it was appropriate, in considering the question of solicitor-client costs, to take into account that the unsuccessful plaintiff was a lawyer.
At p.

369, His Lordship said: Given my findings that the plaintiff did not have a bona fide purpose in bringing the present action but attempted to intimidate and retaliate against the defendants, are solicitor-client costs appropriate?
I have reviewed a leading Alberta decision which extensively reviews the appropriateness of solicitor-client costs—Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.… That case has been summarized in D.R.S.

93-11763 as holding: Where a party's positive misconduct which caused the litigation was calculated to harm the other party, such misconduct must be taken into account on the costs issue notwithstanding the technically proper conduct of the legal proceedings.
While costs lie within the discretion of the court, the discretion must be exercised within the boundaries of sound principles.
The authorities state that in considering the issue, generally the conduct of the proceedings is the primary concern.
The conduct (or misconduct) of the party is of secondary importance unless the misconduct is such that it alone may become the subject of sanctions in costs.
It appears to me that there is also one other factor to consider in the assessment of costs in the present matter.
The plaintiff is a practising lawyer who issued the claim himself.
In these circumstances he utilized the position of responsibility entrusted to him by this province through the Law Society to attempt to intimidate the defendants.
He was in a position where he could, at less expense than a member of the public, force the defendants to incur the expense of hiring counsel.
He cannot say he followed counsel's advice in issuing proceedings.

I noted the many different grounds on which solicitor-client costs have been refused and granted … and it would appear to me that more serious conduct in some cases has not resulted in solicitor-client costs.
However, it appears to me that where the plaintiff is a lawyer, this is a significant consideration.
He took an oath on admission to the Bar to “not promote false suits and frivolous pretences”.

I am satisfied the appropriate disposition of the case is that the defendants should receive their costs on an indemnity basis … Marceau J. has agreed that the fact that the litigant against whom costs are being awarded is a lawyer can be relevant to whether costs should be on a solicitor and client basis.
In C.
C.
L.R.
310–12, His Lordship said: I also think that the fact that the Respondent is a lawyer is relevant and significant in determining that solicitor and client costs should be awarded.
I agree with a case advanced by the Applicant, a decision of Mr.
Justice Marshall in Osborne v.
Pinno… The Respondent here represented himself before and at trial.

As a practising barrister and solicitor in this province and as a member of the Alberta Law Society, he should have been aware that his repeated failure to disclose his financial information to the Applicant would lengthen the proceedings.
As Mr.
Justice Rooke noted in Parkridge Homes Ltd. v.
Anglin (March 15, 1996), Doc.
Calgary 9001-00946 (Alta.

Q.B.), a legally trained individual who represents himself or herself in a court of law is to conduct him or herself consistently with the code expected of member[s] of the Law Society and with his or her status as an officer of the court, gained from that membership.

Notwithstanding that the Respondent was representing himself at trial, he is a practising lawyer and thus an officer of the court… The Respondent in this case, as a self-represented litigant who is legally trained, did not conduct himself in accordance with these principle.

As a member of the Alberta Law Society, the Respondent has a duty to follow the principles and rules outlined in the [Alberta Code of Professional Conduct], even if he is not acting in the capacity of a lawyer.
Because the Respondent knowlingly frustrated the discovery process and unnecessarily lengthened the litigation process, he should be liable to the Applicant for solicitor and client costs.
In Young v.
Young, [1993] 4 S.C.R.
3, Madam Justice McLachlin, speaking for the majority, said at p.
134: Solicitor-client costs are generally awarded only where there has been reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct on the part of one of the parties.
Accordingly, the fact that an application has little merit is no basis for awarding solicitor-client costs; nor is the fact that part of the cost of the litigation may have been paid for by others.
In A.T.U. v.
I.C.T.U.
L.R.
(3d) 207 (Q.B.); [additional reasons at (1998) 59 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 1], Lutz J. said at pp.
212–13: Failure to agree to facts and hindering the pre-trial conference process also constitute appropriate circumstances for the award of solicitor-client costs.
In support of that proposition, Lutz J. made specific reference to the Court of Appeal's decision in 291617 Alberta Ltd. v.
Kretschmer (1997), 193 A.R.
See the annotation headed “Failure to Comply with Directions”, under R.
In Polar Ice Express Inc. v.
Arctic Glacier Inc., 2009 ABCA 20, 2009 CarswellAlta 25, 446 A.R.
L.R.

(4th) 203, the Court, in overturning the costs decision of the learned trial judge, held that, with one possible exception, pre-litigation misconduct cannot be the basis for an award of solicitor-client costs.
At paragraphs 21–22, the Court said: 21 Finally, the appellant objects to solicitor-client costs.
The trial judge said that he was giving these for the appellant's bad pre-suit conduct, and he relied upon Young v.
Young [1993] 4 S.C.R.
In our view, that case is virtually diametrically opposed to that proposition, especially if one looks at the Court of Appeal decision: see p.
41 (N.R., paras.

If that case leaves any doubt on the subject, these other binding authorities hold that in general solicitor-client costs for misconduct must relate to conduct during the suit, not the pre-suit conduct sued over.
See Ludco Ent.
(Ludmer) v.
79); Tree Savers Int. v.
30); Sidorsky v.
CFCN Communications (1997) 206 A.R.
No.
Sign Crafter (1988) v.
Seitanidis, 1998 ABCA 303, [1998] A.R.
Uned.
These are ratio, not obiter.
A few Alberta Queen's Bench decisions briefly state the contrary, but they give few reasons, and cannot overrule the Supreme Court of Canada or the Alberta Court of Appeal.
Some are earlier.
22 Trusts or a fiduciary relationship might be an exception, but that is irrelevant here.
See also: Lee v.
Yeung, 2012 ABQB 102, 2012 CarswellAlta 254 at paras.
Chrystian v.
Topilko, 2010 ABQB 456, 2010 CarswellAlta 1384, 498 A.R.

206, in which Justice Marceau granted full indemnity solicitor-client costs against the Plaintiff who was involved in forging a will and supporting documentation, might be an example of the exception.

Justice Marceau said, at paragraph 59: 59 Having concluded the Plaintiff was complicit in the attempt to perpetrate a fraud upon the court and upon her relatives to benefit her family, the Defendants shall have their costs of all the proceedings, including the applications in court prior to the filing of the Statement of Claim until the discontinuance on a full indemnity basis.

Though Justice Marceau speaks of perpetrating a fraud upon the court (which implies conduct within the litigation), the forging of the will (which was an integral part of the fraud) occurred before the litigation was commenced.
Costs as a deterrent In HSBC Bank Canada v.
1100336 Alberta Ltd., 2012 ABQB 27, 2012 CarswellAlta 37, [2012] 9 W.W.R.

627, Justice Marshall had before him an application respecting costs in a matter where he had previously ruled that “the Defendants [had] engaged in a civil conspiracy to defeat a debt owed by another party to HSBC Bank.
The Bank sought full indemnity costs, and submitted that such an award would act to deter others from engaging in civil conspiracies.
At paragraph 14, his Lordship said: The Bank submits that deterrence to others should be a factor to consider in imposing costs.
The only authority cited is from the criminal law.
I am not satisfied deterrence has a role in civil litigation, outside of promoting timely and efficient prosecution of civil litigation: Rules 1.2, 10.33(2).
However, in Meleshko v.
Alberta, 2013 ABQB 468, 2013 CarswellAlta 1494, 557 A.R.
98, there is reference to deterrence being effected by an award of costs (see paragraph 37).
In that case, the plaintiff was an employee of the Government of Alberta.
The long term disability plan of the government was a self-insured plan which was administered on behalf of the government by Great West Life (GWL).
The plaintiff was receiving benefits under the plan when GWL decided to, and did, discontinue those benefits.
The plaintiff successfully sought judicial review of the GWL decision, and then applied for solicitor-client costs.
In granting solicitor-client costs, Justice Acton said, at paragraphs 32, 37, and 38: 32 I agree with Mr.
Meleshko that GWL was using termination of his benefits to intimidate him into doing things not required of him.
Admittedly in Colborne, solicitor-client costs were awarded because of deceit and dishonesty, and I have not found either here.
However, I conclude that the intimidation of someone who is totally disabled (and whose disability was never questioned) by cutting off their source of income is reprehensible and unconscionable.
Further, I find the decisions in Coughlin and St-Laurent helpful, if not directly applicable.
These were situations in which vulnerable persons were denied insurance benefits, and solicitor-client costs were awarded.
Alberta says that in Coughlin the insurer waited until the 5th day of trial to concede the plaintiff had a disability.
I do not see the point of this distinction.
Alberta and GWL continued to deny Mr.
Meleshko his LTD benefits presumably until the date the decision was released.
While there were no “hardball” tactics used in the course of the judicial review litigation, it is clear from the facts that GWL was indeed playing “hardball” with Mr.

Meleshko leading up to the decision to terminate his benefits. … 37 Here a vulnerable, disabled employee sought the benefits he was entitled to under his contract of employment and was forced to litigate at great expense.

The fact that the litigation concerned a judicial review of a tribunal who was not a Respondent is a “red herring” and ignores the reality that were it not for the actions of Alberta and GWL, there would have been no need to appear before the Appeal Board.
The Respondents should not be permitted to insulate their actions from repercussions for abusing authority.
An award of solicitor-client costs here will hopefully deter GWL from using its powers to intimidate LTD beneficiaries and spur Alberta to ensure that GWL administers the LTD Plan fairly.
38 Justice in this case cannot be accomplished unless there is full indemnification for costs.
Therefore I award solicitor-client costs.
Solicitor-Client Costs When An Adjournment is Sought In Kowdrysh v.
Delong (2001), 310 A.R.
48 (Q.B.), plaintiff's counsel neglected to comply with Rule 218.1, and therefore sought an adjournment of the trial so that the matter could be remedied.
In granting the adjournment, Martin J. awarded solicitor-client costs against the plaintiff's lawyer.
At pp.
51–52, His Lordship said: I also accept that full indemnification costs or solicitor client costs are normally awarded only in exceptional circumstances.

The learned authors, Stevenson and Cote, in their text, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2002), have identified six such circumstances, one of them being (at 460): … as a term of granting some indulgence to the payor, such as extending time, or getting an adjournment, and as a way of curing the prejudice to the other side caused by the delay or reversal or course committed by the party getting the indulgence.
This is such a situation.
The decision of Armstrong v.
Foxridge[(1992), 136 A.R.
243 (Alta.
Q.B.)], provides further authority.

There, the court awarded thrown way costs in circumstances such as these where counsel erred in not providing a 18.1 statement even though he knew, or should have known for a long time, that hat matter was in issue.
Furthermore, common sense and basic principles of fairness apply.
The defendant should not be required to shoulder expenses incurred by an obvious oversight or mistake of opposing counsel.
This is a different situation from the case not being able to be heard because the court's calendar was too crowded, or illness requiring postponement of the trial.
Accordingly, I direct that the defendant be indemnified for all of his costs occasioned by this adjournment.
In Northland Forest Products Ltd. v.
Wood Buffalo (Regional Municipality) (2002), 326 A.R.
311 (Q.B.), Clarke J. in referring to Martin J.'s decision in Kowdrysh v.
Delong (2001), 310 A.R.
48 (Q.B.), said at p.
316: … His case was one where the question of costs was being dealt with where a trial had to be adjourned as a result of counsel's oversight or mistake.

In that context he quotes … from the learned authors Steven & Cote (sic) and adopts the proposition that costs should follow “as a term of granting some indulgence to the payor, such as … an adjournment”.
I have no difficulty with that proposition in a situation where the adjournment is caused by the fault of one party.
I do not subscribe to that proposition where there is no fault since that would mean costs would be granted in every case no matter what the reason for the adjournment.
Solicitor-Client Costs and the Workers' Compensation Board In Nabors Canada LP v.
Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board, Appeals Commission) (2005), 51 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 343 (Q.B.); affirmed (2006) 66 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 199 (C.A.), the widow of a worker killed while engaged in his employment duties had successfully made a claim against the Workers' Compensation Board.
The employer appealed that determination, and the Board successfully applied to be added to the appeal.
Ultimately, the widow succeeded in the appeal, and sought solicitor-client costs.

In granting those costs, Sulyma J. reviewed the general rule of party-party costs, but concluded that the general rule should not apply when a worker (or someone claiming through a worker) is successful against the W.C.B.
Her Ladyship said, at pp.
350–352: The law indicates that, absent exceptional circumstances, the successful party is entitled to party and party costs.
Although this issue remains one of discretion, discretion must be consistent with established principles and practice.
This case did not involve a trial.
However, it did involve an appeal of an administrative decision.
The Appellant Nabors had a statutory right of appeal.
The W.C.B. had an interest in the appeal since the decision appealed from overturned its decision.
Certainly the issues were not frivolous or vexatious, since they arose as a result of recent legislative changes and decisions of this Court.
With respect to the Appellant Nabors, I cannot find that simply as a result of its being a wealthy party it ought to pay higher costs.
I agree with Nabors' submission that the question of whether a party can afford costs is separate and distinct from whether the party opposite is entitled to such an award.
In so finding, I do have regard to the obvious difference in the financial situation of the Respondent widow and a large and profitable corporation.
However, Sitler also argues that the intended nature of the workers' compensation scheme renders this an exceptional circumstances.
As noted by the Supreme Court in Pasiechnyk at para.
26: The importance of the historic trade-off has been recognized by the courts.
In Reference re Validity of Sections 32 and 34 of the Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (1987), 44 D.L.R.
(4th) 501 (Nfld.

C.A.), Goodridge C.J. compared the advantages of workers' compensation against its principal disadvantage: benefits that are paid immediately, whether or not the employer is solvent, and without the costs and uncertainties inherent in the tort system; however, there may be some who would recover more from a tort action than they would under the Act.
(Emphasis added) But, as a result of Nabors' appeal, Sitler has not received the advantage of either immediate benefits or certainty.
Moreover, if she is awarded only party and party costs, she loses the other intended benefit of avoiding the tort system—the avoidance of litigation costs.
Nabors commenced this appeal; Sitler had no choice but to respond or lose the compensation to which she and her children were entitled.
Full indemnification of her costs are necessary in this case for justice to be done.

This is not to suggest that Nabors conducted the litigation in any improper manner, but if the historic trade-off is to continue to provide the advantages intended in return for the possible benefits foregone, litigation expenses should not become a potential bar to successful W.C.B. claimants. … In my view improved access to court review would be illusory if deserving claimants are denied full indemnity for their costs when employers appeal to a court.

Further, the rationale underlying the general rule regarding party and party costs is directly related to the allocation of costs and risk in the tort system; to apply the rule in a system that is expressly intended to be an alternative to the tort system is illogical.
I do, however, view the position of the W.C.B. somewhat differently than that of Nabors.

While I find that Nabors' conduct of the litigation was not inappropriate, I agree with the Respondent's submission that the W.C.B. took contrary positions before this Court in a very short time period and could be said to have re-litigated its position in regards to the standard of review.
Indeed, I am at a loss to reconcile the differing positions.
I cannot do so on the basis that the functional and pragmatic approach dictates that each case must be analyzed on its merits.
I find that the functional and pragmatic approach would in most instances, and certainly in this case, result in the W.C.B. taking a consistent position towards the standard of review.
I say this despite the fact that the analysis of the standard of review must consider the nature of the issue.
In this regard I agree with Sitler's submission that the nature of the issue before the tribunal was exactly the same as that which was before Madam Justice Moreau in Buettner.

I recognize that the W.C.B. is entitled to explore the scope of the standard of review, but the cost of that exploration was not intended to be borne by injured workers, their widows, and children—the intended beneficiaries of the system.
Therefore, the position of the W.C.B. has been abusive, has resulted in attempted re-litigation, and frankly does not serve this party well in its various appearances before the Court.
On this basis there is an exceptional circumstance justifying an increased level of costs, and justice is served by such an award.
I award solicitor-client costs to the Respondent to be shared equally by both the W.C.B. and Nabors.
Costs Associated With Changing Counsel In McAteer v.
Devoncroft Developments Ltd., 2003 ABQB 425, 2003 CarswellAlta 654, 340 A.R.
1, 21 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 115, Rooke J. awarded solicitor/client costs and considered the matter of costs associated with the successful party changing counsel during the course of the litigation.
At p.
156, his Lordship said: When new counsel are retained there is always some work required to “get up to speed” and that is a proper solicitor/client cost, even if it produces some duplication.
While parties should not be encouraged to change counsel repeatedly, changes in counsel do occur from time to time for a variety of reasons.

Unless there is abuse in changing counsel, or some other relevant circumstance exists, none of which was suggested here, the change is reasonable and any costs associated with the change are costs of and within the “four corners of the litigation”, and the losing party should bear them.
Daily Transcripts In Lauzon v.
Davey, 2007 ABQB 121, 2007 CarswellAlta 241, 413 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 306, Gill J. said, at p.
313: The Defendants seek to recover the cost of the court reporters and daily trial transcripts.
The successful party in not usually allowed to recover for daily transcripts see McAteer v.
Devoncroft Developments Ltd., [2003] A.J. no 592 (Alta.
Costs when ex Parte Injunction Set aside In Echo Valley Farms Inc. v.
Alberta (1998), 235 A.R.
394 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Veit discussed the granting of solicitor-client costs when an ex parte injunction is subsequently set aside.
At p.
395 Her Ladyship said: Solicitor-client costs are called for only in unusual situations.
This is one of them.
Principles of fundamental justice require that the court hear from all parties before making decisions.
However, in order to prevent injustice, a court may exceptionally, have to act without hearing from one party.
This dilemma is resolved by placing a heavy burden on the party applying for relief without giving notice to the other interested parties.
The applicant is bound to make full disclosure to the court of all relevant facts and law, including the facts and law that favour the opponent.

Moreover, the applicant assumes the risk that if the court subsequently learns that it was not necessary to apply without giving notice to the other parties, the applicant will be required to pay accelerated costs to the other parties.
Here, Echo Valley knew at least five days prior to the day when it made its ex parte application that the government was intending to cut trees on the road allowance.
It knew that the municipality had a lawyer.
There was no reason to apply to this court for an injunction late on a Friday afternoon without giving notice to the parties on the opposite side.
Costs Where Respondent Takes No Position On Application In B.
B.

(K.), 2011 ABQB 765, 2011 CarswellAlta 2134, the applicant “asked the Director of the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act for access to the departmental file which led to the apprehension of her child”.
The Director took the position the he required a court order, but said he would neither consent to the order nor take a position at the application.
The applicant applied to the Court for the appropriate order, the Director took no position, and the application was granted.
The Court granted the applicant costs.

At paragraphs 7–8, and 11–13, Veit, J. said: 7 The analysis of the applicant's entitlement to costs begins with the commonplace that a court has discretion in the awarding of costs; it is just as clear that judicial discretion in the matter of costs must be exercised judicially.
There is little case law on the specific authority of the court to award costs against a party which has taken no position on an application.
8 Indeed, what authority there is does not award costs against a litigant who takes no position: see decisions cited above.
However, what is noteworthy about those decisions is that, in each of those situations, other than Loney, the party taking no position was only one of two or more respondents on the motion.

In other words, the party requesting some relief had to come to court independently of the party who took no position. … 11 In Alberta, the new Rules of Court provide assistance in answering the applicant's request.
Rule 10.31(1)(a) states that the Court may award

(a) the reasonable and proper costs that a party incurred to file an application, to take proceedings or to carry on an action, or that a party incurred to participate in an application, proceeding or action.

(Emphasis added) 12 Here, because the Director was the only respondent on A.B.'s application, it is obvious that A.B. was required to file an application because the Director refused to consent to the request for access.
Therefore, the plaintiff is entitled to costs against the Director.
13 Nor is this result unfair.

In a situation such as this one, where the Director takes no position, a court might refuse the application; the reality is, however, that without an argument from the Director about why access should be denied, the court is almost certain to grant the order, especially after it has been informed that the Director has vetted the proposed form of order.

The Director may well take the position that his obligation is to protect the confidentiality of the apprehension files; nevertheless, if the Director is aware that the Court is likely to grant access, it could consent to what it may perceive as an inevitable order after having insisted on what it believes are acceptable safeguards.

If the Director chooses not to give consent, but not to argue against the Court's granting of the order, then forcing an applicant to come to court is just another cost which the Director must accept as part of the discharge of his duties.
Costs on Abandoned Applications In T.

Rocky Mountain Play Therapy Institute Inc., 2015 ABQB 61, 2015 CarswellAlta 110 (Master), Master Prowse said at paragraphs 13, 16, and 17: 13 If costs higher than Schedule C costs would have been awarded to a respondent if an application had proceeded and been dismissed, then, in my view, that higher level of costs should be awarded to the respondent if the application is abandoned. … 16 In addition, Schedule C of the Rules of Court specifically contemplates abandoned applications.

Item 7(3) of Schedule C, dealing with contested applications, provides as follows: Abandoned applications: A fee equivalent to 50% of the fee that would be payable under this item if the application had not been abandoned.
17 Therefore my approach is as follows: if the nature of Mr.

Kwan's application, or the manner in which he conducted his application, would have resulted in enhanced or indemnity or penal costs against him upon losing his application, then I should award enhanced or indemnity or penal costs against him upon his abandonment of the application.
Costs for Consent Orders: when “hard work” was involved In GO Community Centre v.

Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203, 2020 CarswellAlta 548, Justice Renke discussed when it is appropriate to award costs for consent orders: [27] In Waterous Investments Inc v Liberton Holdings Inc, [1996] AJ No 334, Justice Veit awarded costs for consent orders, writing as follows at para 23: 23 The plaintiff is entitled to costs for these orders.
The point of the tariff items is to recognize that whether a lawyer initiates a step or responds to a step there is a fee generated for work done.
Unless costs are awarded for those steps, the successful litigant will not receive any assistance in defraying its legal costs for those steps.
This would undermine the very policy objective of costs—to promote reasonable compromise of legal process.

Therefore, a successful litigant is entitled to a recovery of the tariff item for steps taken, even by consent, unless the consent order itself, or the court approving the order, makes a specific costs award for that step.

[28] Justice Veit recounted the following respecting the proceedings before her at paras 11 and 12: 11 Even though this trial involved a maximum claim of $25,000, there were protracted pre-trial processes for which the plaintiff is now claiming costs.
As an example, a law firm which was formerly a defendant in these proceedings brought a motion to pay the deposit into court pending the outcome of the trial.
This was eventually done by consent.
The plaintiff is asking for costs of this interlocutory proceeding.
12 There were protracted dealings between the lawyers on two issues entering the action for trial and security for costs from the plaintiff.
In particular, the defendants' lawyer sent many many letters to the plaintiffs lawyers asking for compliance with agreements made, consent orders given etc.
The plaintiffs then lawyer, not the lawyer appearing on this motion, did not answer this correspondence in a timely way.

[29] Thus, while Justice Veit might be thought to have suggested in para 23 a near-presumption of costs for uncontested applications, the circumstances supporting costs were that counsel had to work hard to get the consent orders and the unsuccessful litigant had not reasonably expedited process.
That is, the circumstances rather than a presumption supported the costs award for consent orders.

[30] In ASC (AB) Facility Inc v Man-Shield (Alta) Construction, 2018 ABQB 855, Justice Antonio, as she then was, commented on Waterous Investments at paras 19 and 20 as follows: [19] It may be possible to debate whether awarding costs for consent orders against one consenting party would encourage or discourage compromise.
In any event, I am unable to read this passage as creating a rule that the party with ultimate success must receive costs for consent orders absent any prior costs award.
There may be circumstances of contention in which hard work was done on one or both sides to reach consent.
There may be other circumstances in which a consent order was reached with little effort, for instance on a pro forma procedural matter.
[20] Absent a fact-specific reason to do so, I am not persuaded that the costs paradigm of “spoils to the victor” should be applied to consent orders.
Therefore this portion of ASC's costs claim is dismissed.
When Waterous Investments is read in context, Justice Antonio's approach is similar to Justice Veit's.
A cost award for even a consent order may be appropriate if “hard work” was necessary to obtain the order or there was some other “fact-specific reason” to award costs for the order.

Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs of Litigation, and Sanctions Division 2.
Recoverable Costs of Litigation Subdivision 1.
General Rule, Considerations and Court Authority
